## The Names of the Angels {#app:names}

Scripture gives the proper names of three holy angels, Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael, and the Church names no others. The Roman synod of 745 confessed that it knew the names of no more than three: *non plus quam trium angelorum nomina cognoscimus, id est Michael, Gabriel, Raphael* (MGH *Conc.* II/1, ed. Werminghoff, 1906, p. 43); Charlemagne’s *Admonitio generalis* of 789 forbade that unknown names be invented or used, *nisi illos quos habemus in auctoritate, id sunt Michahel, Gabrihel, Rafahel* (c. 16, MGH *Capit.* I, ed. Boretius, 1883, p. 55); and the Directory of 2001 teaches that “the practice of assigning names to the Holy Angels should be discouraged, except in the cases of Gabriel, Raphael and Michael whose names are contained in Holy Scripture” (*Directory on Popular Piety* 217). The acts are expounded in §[23](#sec:devotion).

The word “angel” is itself a name of office. Gregory teaches, *angelorum vocabulum, nomen est officii, non naturae*, and Isidore repeats it, *Angelorum autem vocabulum officii nomen est, non naturae. Semper enim spiritus sunt, sed cum mittuntur, vocantur angeli* (Gregory, *Hom. in Ev.* 34.8; Isidore, *Etym.* VII.5.2). The proper names are names of office too. In the heavenly city, Gregory says, the angels do not take names in order to be known, for the vision of God makes all known; *sed cum ad nos aliquid ministraturi veniunt, apud nos etiam nomina a ministeriis trahunt*: when they come to us on some ministry, they take their names among us from their ministries (*Hom. in Ev.* 34.8).

### The Three Names of Scripture

| **Name** | **Scripture (Vulgate)** | **Meaning as the Fathers give it** | **In the Roman liturgy** |
|:-----------|:----------------|:-----------------|:-------------------|
| Michael | Dan 10:13, 21; 12:1; Jude 9; Apoc 12:7 | *Quis ut Deus* (Gregory, *Hom. in Ev.* 34.9); *qui interpretatur quis sicut Deus* (Jerome, *In Dan.* 8:16); *Qui sicut Deus* (Isidore, *Etym.* VII.5.12) | 29 September; 8 May (pre-1955); Confiteor; incense prayer; Offertory of the Requiem; Litany |
| Gabriel | Dan 8:16; 9:21; Luke 1:19, 26 | *fortitudo Dei* (Gregory, *Hom. in Ev.* 34.9); *fortitudo, vel robustus Dei* (Jerome, *In Dan.* 8:16); *fortitudo Dei* (Isidore, *Etym.* VII.5.10) | 24 March (pre-1955, 1962); 29 September (postconciliar); the Angelus; Litany |
| Raphael | Tob 3:25; 5:5; 12:15 | *medicina Dei* (Gregory, *Hom. in Ev.* 34.9); *curatio; vel medicina Dei* (Jerome, *In Dan.* 8:16); *curatio vel medicina Dei* (Isidore, *Etym.* VII.5.13) | 24 October (pre-1955, 1962); 29 September (postconciliar); Litany |

The Fathers read each name as the sign of the angel’s work. For Gregory, whenever a work of wondrous power is to be done Michael is sent, so that by the deed and the name it may be understood *quia nullus potest facere quod facere praevalet Deus*, that no one can do what God can do; and the old enemy who in his pride desired to be like God, saying *similis ero Altissimo*, will at the end of the world be slain by Michael and learn *quia ad Dei similitudinem per superbiam nullus exsurgat*. Gabriel, the Strength of God, is sent to Mary because he came to announce the one who came humble to war against the powers of the air, the *Dominus fortis et potens, Dominus potens in praelio* of the psalm. Raphael is the Medicine of God because he touched the eyes of Tobias as a physician and wiped away the darkness of his blindness (Gregory, *Hom. in Ev.* 34.9; read in the Breviary on 29 September, §[22](#sec:liturgy)). Jerome, commenting on Daniel’s vision, gives the same three offices in other words: Gabriel, *qui praepositus est praeliis*, is sent where wars and the succession of kingdoms are at issue; wherever healing is needed, *Raphael mittitur*; and where propitiation or expiation is needed, *Michael dirigitur, qui interpretatur quis sicut Deus* (Jerome, *In Dan.* 8:16, PL 25). Isidore gathers the whole into his *Etymologies*: where divine power or strength is shown, Gabriel is sent; when a work of wondrous power is done, Michael; wherever there is need of healing, Raphael (*Etym.* VII.5.10–14).

Scripture gives Raphael a second name in the book of Tobias, the name he took in his disguise: “I am Azarias the son of the great Ananias” (Tob 5:18). The sermon the Breviary for England reads under Augustine’s name on Raphael’s feast comments: “The Angel hid his name from you; he said not, I am the Angel Raphael, but, I am Azarias, the son of Ananias the Great. In the first name that he gave thee he hid his high estate, lest he should scare him that hired him” (Bute, IV, p. 686).

### The Titles of Michael in the Liturgy

| **Title** | **Where the Church uses it** | **Scripture behind it** |
|:-------------|:------------------------|:----------------------------|
| *Princeps militiae Angelorum*; “Prince of the heavenly host” | Responsory of 29 September (*BR*); prayer after Low Mass (“O Prince of the heavenly host”) | Dan 10:13, 21; 12:1; Apoc 12:7 |
| *Praepositus paradisi*, “the Vice-Roy of Paradise” | Antiphon and responsory of 29 September (*BR*; Bute, IV, p. 594) | — |
| *Salutis signifer*; *signifer sanctus Michael* | Vespers hymn of 29 September; Offertory of the Mass for the Dead | Apoc 12:7–9 |
| *Angelus pacis* | Lauds hymn of 29 September | — |
| *Dei nuntius pro animabus justis*; prince *super omnes animas suscipiendas* | Antiphons of 29 September | Luke 16:22 |
| *Princeps gloriosissime* | Magnificat antiphon of 29 September; *Raccolta* n. 289 | — |
| “Prince of the Church of Jesus Christ” | Versicle of the chaplet (*Raccolta* n. 291) | Dan 12:1 |

### The Names of the Fallen in Scripture

Scripture gives the fallen angels names that are titles of their revolt and of their work. The Church uses them as Scripture does.

| **Name** | **Scripture (Douay)** | **Reading** |
|:-------------|:------------------------|:----------------------------|
| Satan | “Satan also was present among them” (Job 1:6); “that old serpent, who is called the devil and Satan” (Apoc 12:9) | The accuser: “the accuser of our brethren is cast forth” (Apoc 12:10) |
| The devil (*diabolus*) | “to be tempted by the devil” (Matt 4:1); Apoc 12:9 | The tempter of Christ, “who seduceth the whole world” (Apoc 12:9) |
| The dragon, the old serpent | Apoc 12:7–9 | “that old serpent,” cast out by Michael and his angels (Apoc 12:9) |
| Beelzebub | “Beelzebub the prince of the devils” (Matt 12:24) | The name the Pharisees used for the prince of the demons |
| Abaddon, Apollyon, *Exterminans* | “the angel of the bottomless pit (whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon and in Greek Apollyon, in Latin Exterminans)” (Apoc 9:11) | The king over the locusts of the abyss (Apoc 9:3–11) |
| Asmodeus | “a devil named Asmodeus” (Tob 3:8) | The demon bound by Raphael (Tob 8:3) |
| Belial | “what concord hath Christ with Belial?” (2 Cor 6:15) | Set by the Apostle over against Christ |
| The prince of this world | “now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John 12:31) | The dominion broken by the Cross (§[18](#sec:assaults)) |
| Lucifer | “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who didst rise in the morning?” (Isa 14:12) | Applied by the Fathers to the devil’s fall: Origen, *De principiis* I.5.5; Gregory, *Hom. in Ev.* 34.9 on Isa 14:13–14 |

The prophet speaks to the king of Babylon, and the Fathers read in his fall the fall of the first rebel. Origen argues from the name itself: “Most evidently by these words is he shown to have fallen from heaven, who formerly was Lucifer, and who used to arise in the morning. For if, as some think, he was a nature of darkness, how is Lucifer said to have existed before? Or how could he arise in the morning, who had in himself nothing of the light?” (Origen, *De principiis* I.5.5, trans. Crombie, ANF 4). The name of the light-bearer is thus a witness to the doctrine the Church defined against the dualists: the devil was created good and became evil of himself (Lateran IV, DS 800; §[2](#sec:faith); §[13](#sec:fall)). Scripture adds that “Satan himself transformeth himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor 11:14).

### Names from the Apocryphal Books

The fourth book of Esdras, which the Douay Bible of 1610 printed after the canonical books “because they are not receiued into the Canon of Diuine Scriptures by the Catholique Church,” names two angels: “the Angel answered me, that was sent to me, whose name was Vriel,” and “Ieremiel the Archangel answered to those things” (4 Esdras 4:1, 36, Douay 1610 appendix). Isidore received the first name into his *Etymologies*: *Vriel interpretatur ignis Dei, sicut legimus apparuisse ignem in rubo* (*Etym.* VII.5.15). The first book of Enoch gives seven “names of the holy angels who watch”: Uriel, Raphael, Raguel, Michael, Saraqâêl, Gabriel, and Remiel (1 En 20:1–8, trans. Charles, 1917; §[3](#sec:before-christ)). The names that stand only in these books are graded Apocryphal.

### The Names the Roman Synod of 745 Rejected

Aldebert’s prayer, read before Pope Zachary’s synod, invoked eight angels by name: *angelus Uriel, angelus Raguel, angelus Tubuel, angelus Michael, angelus Adinus, angelus Tubuas, angelus Sabaoc, angelus Simiel* (MGH *Conc.* II/1, p. 42). The synod judged that of these only Michael was an angel, and that under the names of angels Aldebert had invoked demons, *sub obtentu angelorum demonum nomina introduxit* (ibid., p. 43).

| **Name** | **Other witness** | **Disposition** |
|:-------------|:------------------------|:----------------------------|
| Uriel | 4 Esdras 4:1 (“Vriel”); Isidore, *Etym.* VII.5.15 | Rejected by the Roman synod of 745; Apocryphal |
| Raguel | 1 En 20:4 (§[3](#sec:before-christ)) | Rejected by the Roman synod of 745; Apocryphal |
| Tubuel, Adinus, Tubuas, Sabaoc, Simiel | Known from Aldebert’s prayer | Rejected by the Roman synod of 745 as names of demons |
| Michael | Dan 10:13; Jude 9; Apoc 12:7 | The one angel’s name in the prayer; a name of Scripture |

The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith applied the same rule in 1983 and 1992 to names of angels drawn from presumed private revelations, which may be neither taught nor used in prayer (decree of 6 June 1992, AAS 84 \[1992\] 805–806; §[23](#sec:devotion)).

## The Demons’ Powers and Their Limits {#app:demons}

The demons keep the natural powers of the angelic nature (*ST* I q. 64 a. 1); their will is fixed in evil (a. 2); and every use of their power falls under the command, permission, or restraint of God. Gregory states the rule: “the will of Satan is always evil, but his power is never unjust, for his will he derives from himself, but his power he derives from God” (*Moralia* II.10.17). Augustine gives the double limit, of permission and of nature: a man “can walk, yet … cannot do so if he is not permitted; but … cannot fly, even if he be permitted” (*De Trin.* III.9.18). The rites and discipline of exorcism belong to the study *Catholic Exorcism: History, Discipline, and Pastoral Practice*.

| **Power** | **What the demons can do** | **Limit under God** | **Aquinas** | **Fathers and the Church** |
|:--------|:---------------|:----------------|:---------|:---------------|
| **Natural knowledge** | Keep their natural knowledge whole; the angelic gifts “exist, and are complete, and all luminous” in them | Speculative knowledge by grace is lessened to what is revealed; affective knowledge and charity are lost; they knew the Incarnation less fully; error is possible in what exceeds nature | *ST* I q. 64 a. 1; *De malo* q. 16 a. 6 | Dionysius, *DN* 4.23; Damascene, *De fide orth.* II.4 (“they know the Scriptures”); Augustine, *De div. daem.* 6.10 |
| **Knowledge of the future** | Foreknow by conjecture what proceeds from causes usually or necessarily; foretell by speed and observation, and often what they themselves are about to do | The future in itself is known to God alone; they are deceived when a higher command overturns their plans, and they deceive from envy | *ST* I q. 57 a. 3; *De malo* q. 16 a. 7 | Athanasius, *Vita Antonii* 31–33; Damascene, *De fide orth.* II.4; Augustine, *De div. daem.* 5.9–6.10 |
| **Knowledge of thoughts** | Learn thoughts in their effects, from signs in the body and bearing, and explore a man’s disposition by temptation | The thought as it is in the will is known only to God and to the one who wills | *ST* I q. 57 a. 4; q. 114 a. 2 ad 2; *De malo* q. 16 a. 8 | Cassian, *Conl.* VII.15–16; Augustine, *De div. daem.* 5.9, qualified in *Retract.* II.30 |
| **Imagination and senses** | Move the imagination through the spirits and humours, sleeping or waking; present sensible objects outwardly; change the senses from within; rouse the passions | Cannot impress a form never received from sense (“a man born blind”); cannot infuse species into the intellect; the will remains free to consent or resist | *ST* I q. 111 aa. 2–4; *De malo* q. 16 aa. 11–12 | Augustine, *De civ. Dei* XVIII.18; Cassian, *Conl.* VII.8; Origen, *De princ.* III.2.4 |
| **Local motion of bodies** | Move bodies locally, including bodies not joined to them, and through local motion apply natural agents | Cannot induce a substantial form immediately; create nothing; do not rule the weather by their own authority; act only as far as permitted | *ST* I q. 110 aa. 2–3; *De malo* q. 16 aa. 9–10 | Braga I, can. 8 (DS 458); Augustine, *De Trin.* III.8.13, III.9.18; Damascene, *De fide orth.* II.3–4 |
| **Wonders** | Produce real effects by applying the “seeds” in the elements, as the serpents and frogs of Pharaoh’s magicians and the fire and wind against Job; work illusions on the senses | No miracle in the proper sense; no man turned into a beast and no dead man raised; the magicians failed at the gnats, “the finger of God” | *ST* I q. 110 a. 4; q. 114 a. 4; *SCG* III.103; *De pot.* q. 6 a. 5 | Augustine, *De Trin.* III.7.12–8.13, *De civ. Dei* XVIII.18, XX.19; Exod 8:18–19 |
| **Temptation** | Tempt to sin as their proper office; persuade and kindle thoughts; the devil is the indirect cause of all sins through the first sin | Cannot force the will; not the direct cause of every sin; not beyond a man’s strength; the Powers restrain them; the conquered withdraw for a time | *ST* I q. 111 a. 2; q. 114 aa. 1–3, 5 | Origen, *De princ.* III.2.2–3; Cassian, *Conl.* VII.8, 20, 22; Gregory, *Moralia* II.10–11, *Hom. in Ev.* 34.10; 1 Cor 10:13 |
| **Dominion over fallen man** | By Adam’s sin man fell into captivity under the devil’s power | Broken by Christ’s victory; Satan’s power is a creature’s and not infinite, and permitted by providence | *ST* I q. 114 a. 1 | Trent, DS 1511, 1521; CCC 395, 2853; Athanasius, *Vita Antonii* 28, 41; Col 2:15 |

The remedies the Fathers name are the weapons of the Christian life. Antony sums them up: the demons “fear the fasting, the sleeplessness, the prayers, the meekness, the quietness, the contempt of money and vainglory, the humility, the love of the poor, the alms, the freedom from anger of the ascetics, and, chief of all, their piety towards Christ” (*Vita Antonii* 30). Paul VI gave the same answer: *tutto ciò che ci difende dal peccato ci ripara per ciò stesso dall’invisibile nemico. La grazia è la difesa decisiva*, whatever defends us from sin shields us by that very fact from the invisible enemy; grace is the decisive defence (audience of 15 November 1972).

| **Remedy** | **Scripture (Douay)** | **Fathers** | **Aquinas and the Church** |
|:-----------|:----------------|:-----------------|:-------------------|
| The Cross | “despoiling the principalities and powers” (Col 2:15) | Athanasius, *Vita Antonii* 23, 35 (“they are cowards, and greatly fear the sign of the Lord’s Cross”); *De incarnatione* 47.2 (“by the Sign of the Cross, though a man but use it, he drives out their deceits”); Cassian, *Conl.* VII.23, VIII.18 | CCC 2853: the victory “won once for all at the Hour” of the Passion |
| The name of Jesus | “The devils also are subject to us in thy name” (Luke 10:17); “In my name they shall cast out devils” (Mark 16:17); Phil 2:10 | Athanasius, *Vita Antonii* 40–41; Origen, *Contra Celsum* I.6 (“Such power, indeed, does the name of Jesus possess over evil spirits”); Augustine, *De div. qq. 83* q. 79.4 | *ST* I q. 110 a. 4 ad 2: the signs of public justice, “as by invoking the name of Christ” |
| Prayer and fasting | “This kind can go out by nothing, but by prayer and fasting” (Mark 9:28\[29\]); “Watch ye: and pray that ye enter not into temptation” (Matt 26:41); Matt 6:13 | Athanasius, *Vita Antonii* 23 (“by prayer, fasting, and faith in the Lord their attack immediately fails”), 30 | CCC 2849: the battle and the victory “become possible only through prayer”; Paul VI, 15 November 1972, on Mark 9:28\[29\] |
| Faith, humility, and resistance | “Taking the shield of faith” (Eph 6:16); “Whom resist ye, strong in faith” (1 Pet 5:9); “resist the devil: and he will fly from you” (Jas 4:7) | Antony’s counsel to rejoice in the Lord and despise the enemy (*Vita Antonii* 42); Cassian, *Conl.* VII.8; Origen, *De princ.* III.2.3–4 | *ST* I q. 111 a. 2: the will “ever remains free to consent to, or to resist” |
| Grace and the sacraments | “that, through death, he might destroy him who had the empire of death” (Heb 2:14) | Chrysostom, *Hom. in Ioann.* 46: “Let us then return from that table like lions breathing fire, having become terrible to the devil”; Ambrose to the newly baptized, in CCC 2852 | Trent on the captivity from which justification frees (DS 1511, 1521); *ST* I q. 114 a. 1 ad 2: the recompense gained “principally through the grace of God” |
| The holy angels | “Fear not: for there are more with us than with them” (4 Kgs 6:16); Ps 33\[34\]:8; Ps 90\[91\]:11 | Origen, *De princ.* III.2.5 (the angel who stands with Jacob in the struggle); Gregory, *Hom. in Ev.* 34.10 (the Powers bridle the adverse powers), *Moralia* XVII.13.19 | *ST* I q. 114 a. 1 ad 2: “secondarily through the guardianship of the angels”; §[17](#sec:guardians) |

## Positions on the First Sin {#app:first-sin}

Lateran IV fixes what the faith holds: the devil and the other demons were created good by nature and became evil of themselves (*ipsi per se facti sunt mali*, DS 800). The witnesses below, in chronological order, state in their own words what the sin was in its object and when it was committed; §[20.6](#sec:dq-firstsin) expounds their division.

| **Witness** | **Locus** | **Object of the sin** | **Moment and cause** |
|:-----------|:----------------|:-----------------|:-------------------|
| Gregory of Nazianzus | *Or.* 38.9–10 | Pride: Lucifer “became and is called Darkness through his pride”; his hosts “creators of evil by their revolt against good” | After the angelic world’s creation and before the visible world’s (38.9–10); by their own movement toward evil |
| Augustine | *De civ. Dei* XI.13–15; XII.6–7 | Pride: forsaking God and turning to themselves, “the beginning of sin” (XII.6, citing Ecclus 10:15) | Not from the beginning of his created existence but “from the beginning of his sin” (XI.15, on 1 John 3:8); the evil will has no efficient cause (XII.7) |
| John of Damascus | *De fide orth.* II.3–4 | Rebellion: set over the earthly realm, he “determined to rise in rebellion” against God, the first to depart from good (II.4) | Of his free choice, after his making by the good Creator; for angels the fall is as death, admitting no repentance (II.4) |
| Anselm | *De casu diaboli* c. 4 | He willed *aliquod commodum, quod nec habebat nec tunc velle debuit*; thereby *voluit inordinate similis esse deo*, by a will *nulli subdita*, subject to none | By his own will, after creation; the object was what he would have reached had he stood fast |
| Peter Lombard | *Sent.* II d. 5 c. 1 | Pride, the mother of envy: *voluerunt se parificare Deo* | *Post creationem mox*: aversion by free will; the converting grace given to those who stood was never given to those who fell |
| Bonaventure | *In II Sent.* d. 5 a. 1 q. 1; d. 4 a. 1 q. 2 | Pride: presumption at the sight of his own beauty; ambition to preside over the rest by his own authority, subject to none (*aequiparantia*); confirmed in envy and hatred | At once upon beholding himself; grace had more probably not been given in the first instant (d. 4 a. 1 q. 2) |
| Aquinas | *ST* I q. 63 aa. 2–3, 5–6; *De malo* q. 16 aa. 3–4 | Pride: likeness to God in seeking final beatitude *per virtutem suae naturae… sine Deo gratiam conferente*; not equality, which he knew to be impossible | Not in the first instant (rejected by the masters as erroneous, a. 5; his reason: the first instant is the turn to natural self-knowledge); at once after it, if created in grace (a. 6) |
| Scotus | *Ord.* II d. 6 qq. 1–2 | An inordinate friendship-love of self, then immoderate desire of beatitude; *non fuit superbia proprie dicta… magis videtur reduci ad luxuriam*; equality with God only by an inefficacious volition of complacency (q. 1) | The will’s first inordinate act, an elicited free act following the order of *velle amicitiae* before *velle concupiscentiae* (q. 2) |
| Suárez | *De angelis* VII.13–14, 28–30 | De facto, and very probably: pride desiring the hypostatic union for his own nature, and envious opposition to Christ from the beginning (VII.13 n. 13) | Upon the revelation of Christ as the angels’ head and the author of grace (VII.30); a positive precept laid on them is probable (VII.28) |

All the witnesses hold the frame of *Firmiter*: a spiritual creature, made good, turning from God by its own will, with pride in the broad sense as the sin’s name. They divide on the object — likeness to God in beatitude by natural power (Anselm, Aquinas), equality or self-sufficient preeminence (Lombard, Bonaventure), inordinate self-love (Scotus), the hypostatic union (Suárez) — and on the moment, whether the sin could fall in the first instant of creation and how soon after it the fall is to be placed. That the fall was the angels’ own is Defined (DS 800); its object and its moment are Disputed among the schools (§[20.6](#sec:dq-firstsin)).

## Terminology {#app:terminology}

The English terms this reference prefers, with the Latin and Greek of the sources and the loci that fix the usage. English *Summa* wording follows the English Dominican translation; the Latin follows the Leonine text; Greek is transliterated.

|:-----------|:---------------|:-----------|:-------------------------|

| **advantage** | *commodum* | *—* | The object of the will for happiness; happiness is made of advantages (Anselm, *De casu diaboli* 4, 12–14) |
| **adverse powers** | *virtutes adversae* | *—* | Restrained by the order of Powers (Gregory, *Hom.* 34.10) |
| **aevum** | *aevum* | *aion* | Angelic duration between time and eternity; also “aeon” (*ST* I q. 61 a. 2; cf. *In II Sent.* d. 2 q. 1 a. 1; Bonaventure, *De sanctis Angelis* 5) |
| **affective knowledge** | *cognitio affectiva* | *—* | *producens amorem Dei*; English Dominican “effective” (*ST* I q. 64 a. 1 co.) |
| **after the image / after the likeness** | *ad imaginem / ad similitudinem* | *kat’ eikona / kath’ homoiōsin* | Palamas, *Cap.* 39, 62–64; *ST* I q. 93 a. 3 |
| **ally** | *—* | *symmachia* | The angel “brother” to the mind, “set beside … as an ally” (Gregory of Nyssa, *De vita Moysis* II; PG 44, 337D) |
| **angel** | *angelus* | *angelos* | A name of office, not of nature: *nomen officii, non naturae* (Gregory), *officii nomen* (Augustine, whose words the Catechism gives); Gregory: “Graeca etenim lingua angeli nuntii”; Isidore gives the Hebrew “malachoth” (Mal 3:1; *CH* 4–5; *ST* I q. 108 a. 5 ad 1; Augustine, *Enarr. in Ps.* 103, s. 1.15; *De civ. Dei* XV.23; Gregory, *Hom. in Ev.* 34.8; Isidore, *Etym.* VII.5.1–2; *Sent.* I.10.1; Rabanus, *De universo* I.5; CCC 329) |

| **spiritual substance, a body of its own kind** | *substantia spiritalis … corporis alicuius, sui tamen generis* | *—* | Tertullian’s own view; contrast *ST* I q. 50 a. 1 (Tertullian, *De carne Christi* 6.9) |
| **standard-bearer** | *signifer* | *—* | “salutis signifer” (Requiem Offertory; *Te splendor*) |
| **stewards and tutors** | *actores et tutores* | *—* | Gal 4:2; Bernard, *In Ps. Qui habitat* 12.7 |
| **stronger nature** | *natura potior* | *—* | The angels relative to man (Hilary, *Tract. in Ps.* 134.17) |
| **subsisting form** | *forma subsistens* | *—* | Form existing without matter (*ST* I q. 50 a. 2 ad 3; a. 5 co.) |
| **subtlety and tenuity (of demons)** | *subtilitas et tenuitas* | *—* | ANF “subtleness and tenuity” (Tertullian, *Apol.* 22.5) |
| **subtlety of nature; experience of times** | *subtilitas naturae; experientia temporum* | *—* | “experience” by similitude only (*ST* I q. 58 a. 3 ad 3; Isidore, *Sent.* I.10.17) |
| **sudden acceptance of truth** | *per subitam acceptionem veritatis* | *—* | Angelic choice without counsel (*ST* I q. 59 a. 3 ad 1) |
| **summit of things** | *in summo rerum vertice* | *—* | Intellectual creatures (*SCG* II.46 n. 1) |
| **supernatural beatitude** | *beatitudo supernaturalis* | *—* | Beatitude beyond natural faculty, by charity (*ST* I q. 60 a. 5 ad 4; q. 62 a. 1) |
| **surrounding circle of angels** | *angelorum circumstantia* | *—* | Tertullian, *De orat.* 3.3 |
| **synaxis** | *synaxis* | *synaxis* | “attention, concord, union” (*Synaxarium CP*, 8 Nov.) |
| **theurgy** | *theurgia* | *theurgia* | Rejected as demon-worship under angels’ names (Augustine, *De civ. Dei* X.9–10; Iamblichus, *De myst.* II.3) |
| **threefold cord** | *funiculus triplex* | *—* | The angels’ love: for God, for us, for themselves (Bernard, *In festo S. Michaelis* 1.4) |
| **thrice-holy hymn** | *Trisagium* | *Trisagion* | Maximus uses it also of the Sanctus (Maximus, *Myst.* 13, 19; Hapgood p. 86) |
| **Thrones** | *Throni; sedes* | *thronoi* | Called *sedes* (Gregory, Isidore); God sits in them and decrees judgments (Col 1:16; *CH* 7.1; Gregory, *Hom.* 34.10; Isidore, *Etym.* VII.5.21) |
| **to assist / to minister** | *assistere; ministrare; administrare* | *—* | To stand by; assisting is proper to the first hierarchy (Dan 7:10; Gregory, *Hom.* 34.12; *Moralia* XVII.13.18; Isidore, *Etym.* VII.5.19; *In II Sent.* d. 10 q. 1 a. 1; *ST* I q. 112 a. 3) |
| **to enter (the mind)** | *illabi (menti)* | *—* | Proper to God alone (Gennadius, *De eccl. dogm.* 83; *ST* I q. 56 a. 2 obj. 3) |
| **to tempt** | *tentare* | *—* | “To make trial”, *experimentum sumere* (*ST* I q. 114 a. 2) |
| **tongue of angels** | *lingua Angelorum* | *—* | Metaphor for the power of manifesting the concept (*ST* I q. 107 a. 1 ad 2) |
| **transverberation** | *—* | *—* | The received name of Teresa’s vision (Teresa, *Life* 29.16–17) |
| **tutor** | *paedagogus* | *paidagōgos* | Of the believer; CCC 336 renders Basil’s sentence with “protector” (Basil, *Adv. Eun.* III.1; PG 29, 656B; Bernard, *In Ps. Qui habitat* 12.3) |
| **types of the divine works** | *rationes divinorum operum* | *—* | Known the more, the more perfectly God is seen (*ST* I q. 106 a. 1 ad 1) |
| **union by pressure from without** | *applicatio et oppressio* | *—* | How demons act on the possessed (Gennadius, *De eccl. dogm.* 83) |
| **universal matter** | *materia universalis* | *—* | Avicebron (*ST* I q. 50 a. 2 co.; *De sub. sep.* c. 5) |
| **upper, middle, lower classes of a city** | *optimates; populus honorabilis; vilis populus* | *—* | English Dominican “nobles, middle-class, common people” (*ST* I q. 108 a. 2 co.) |
| **vestibule of God** | *in vestibulis Dei* | *—* | First hierarchy; Parker “Its very vestibule” (*ST* I q. 108 a. 1 co.; *CH* 7.2) |
| **Vice-Roy of Paradise** | *praepositus paradisi* | *—* | Bute’s rendering (*BR*, 29 Sept.) |
| **virtual contact** | *contactus virtutis* | *—* | English Dominican “virtual contact” (*ST* I q. 53 a. 1 co.) |
| **virtual quantity** | *quantitas virtualis* | *—* | Contrasted with dimensive quantity (*ST* I q. 52 a. 1 co.) |
| **Virtues** | *Virtutes* | *dynameis* | Channel of miracles (Gregory), through whom signs and miracles are done (*ST* I q. 110 a. 4 obj. 1); also the common name of all the heavenly spirits, as in Jerome’s *Virtutes Dei*, “Powers of God”; Parker renders “Powers”, a source of confusion with the Powers, *potestates* (Eph 1:21; 1 Pet 3:22; *CH* 8.1; *ST* I q. 108 a. 5 ad 1; Gregory, *Hom.* 34.10; Isidore, *Etym.* VII.5.17; Jerome, *Ep.* 18.17) |
| **ward** | *alumnus* | *—* | “pray for his ward” (Suárez, *De angelis* VI.17) |
| **watch-tower of the angels** | *specula angelorum* | *—* | Rendered “watch” (Hilary, *Tract. in Ps.* 137.5) |
| **watcher** | *vigil* | *ir* | Jerome: signifies angels “quod semper vigilent”; Douay “watcher”; *ir* is Theodotion’s transliteration of the Aramaic; the Enochic books’ name for angels holy and fallen; Ephrem’s usual name for the angels (Dan 4:10, 14 \[4:13, 17\]; Jerome, *In Dan.* 4:10; Ephrem, *Nat.* I, XIV; *Epiph.* IV, VI, VIII; cf. Hesiod, *WD* 252–255) |
| **wayfarer / comprehensor** | *viator / comprehensor* | *—* | The blessed angels are *comprehensores*, not *viatores*; guardianship lasts “quandiu viator est” (*ST* I q. 62 a. 9; q. 113 a. 4) |
| **will** | *voluntas* | *—* | Inclination following intellectual apprehension of good in general (*ST* I q. 59 a. 1) |
| **will for happiness** | *voluntas beatitudinis* | *—* | Tempered by justice without losing the power to exceed (Anselm, *De casu diaboli* 13–14) |

## Witness Register {#app:witnesses}

Every author and every act that this treatise cites as a witness appears here once. Scripture, the Jewish writings outside the canon, and the philosophers come first; then the councils, popes, and Roman congregations by date; the Fathers and Doctors by date; Thomas Aquinas and the later scholastics; the saints and spiritual writers; and the liturgical books. “Standing” gives the Church’s recognition of the person, or the kind of the act. A Doctor of the Church is named with the proclaiming pope and the year, as the act or another Holy See document records them or, for proclamations before 1909, the *Catholic Encyclopedia*’s article “Doctors of the Church”; the year is omitted where it is uncertain. The four Latin Doctors are dated by Boniface VIII’s decree of 1298 ordering their feasts kept as doubles in the whole Church, and the four Greek Doctors by the Breviary of Pius V (1568), which raised their feasts to the same rank. Where no such title applies, the column says “Father,” “saint,” or what the witness was. Standing describes the witness; the grade of a teaching stands with the teaching where it is stated. “Works read” names the works read at their own loci, whose editions and translations are listed in Appendix [P](#app:references); “Where treated” gives the sections and appendices that expound or cite each witness.

## Scope, Corpus, and Qualifications {#app:scope}

##### Question and reader.

This reference asks what the Catholic tradition, as Saint Thomas Aquinas systematized it, holds about the angels: what they are, how they know and will, how they were made and how some fell, how they are ordered, and what they do for the world and for man; and on what authority each part rests. It is written for a Catholic reader, student, or teacher who wants that teaching in the order of the *Summa theologiae*, with the Scriptures, the Fathers, and the saints from whom Aquinas received it and in whom the Church has lived it.

##### Corpus and completeness.

The systematic spine is *ST* I qq. 50–64 and *ST* I qq. 106–114. Every article of those twenty-four questions is treated in the body and listed once in the article census (Appendix [D](#app:census)); other articles of the *Summa* enter where the treatise points to them. The *Celestial Hierarchy* is expounded in all fifteen of its chapters, but not reproduced. Fathers and Doctors are read at their own loci rather than through the *Summa*’s quotation of them; a view reported only as Aquinas reports it is attributed to Aquinas’s citation. The Greek and Latin Fathers before Dionysius, Augustine, and the Fathers and Doctors after him receive their own expositions, and the saints and spiritual writers of later centuries enter for the Church’s lived devotion to the angels. Later school authors and the Byzantine tradition enter as witnesses to named questions at identified loci. Magisterial acts are those that teach or regulate belief and devotion concerning the angels; liturgical claims name the rite, book, calendar, and rank. Handbooks and encyclopedias served only to locate texts.

##### Grades of authority.

Each doctrinal proposition carries one of seven grades, which describe the standing of the proposition and not the weight of its author:

Defined<br>
taught by a conciliar definition or a profession of faith;

Church teaching<br>
taught by the ordinary magisterium, the Catechism, or a papal act, without a definition;

Common teaching<br>
held commonly by the Fathers and theologians, without a magisterial act that teaches it;

Thomist position<br>
Aquinas’s determination where another Catholic school determines otherwise;

Disputed<br>
an open question on which the witnesses divide without a prevailing common teaching;

Pious tradition<br>
devotional tradition received in the Church’s life, such as the lives of the saints and the apparitions the Church honours in her calendar; and

Apocryphal<br>
material from writings outside the canon, stated as such.

The grade is the compiler’s judgement; its basis is the act or witness cited beside it. Where the witnesses do not settle a grade, the lower grade is given and the reason stands with the claim. Each question of the *Summa* closes with a frame giving the governing loci, the grades with their basis, the authorities the articles invoke together with the further witnesses read, and any contrary opinion.

##### Texts, translations, and terminology.

English quotations of the *Summa* follow the translation of the Fathers of the English Dominican Province (second revised edition, 1920) as presented by New Advent; Latin key terms follow the Leonine text as presented by the Corpus Thomisticum. The *Celestial Hierarchy* is quoted in John Parker’s translation (London and Oxford, 1899) and addressed by chapter and section. Scripture is cited by the books, chapters, and verses of the Vulgate, with the Hebrew numbering in brackets where it differs, and quoted from the Douay–Rheims Bible in Challoner’s revision. In its own prose the book names the persons of the Old Testament in the Douay forms (Isaias, Ezechiel, Eliseus, Osee); quotations keep the forms of their translators. The Fathers are quoted from the Ante-Nicene and Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series where those translations exist, and otherwise rendered by the compiler from an identified Latin or Greek edition. Where no public-domain English exists, as for the Latin of the councils and the Italian of recent papal addresses, the English is the compiler’s own and the original words stand beside it in italics. Greek terms are given in italic transliteration. Appendix [M](#app:terminology) records the preferred English terms with their Latin and Greek.

##### Attribution of the Dionysian corpus.

The corpus bears the name of Dionysius the Areopagite, Saint Paul’s convert at Athens (Acts 17:34), and under that name the Church of East and West received it: Gregory the Great, John Damascene, and Aquinas cite it as the Areopagite’s. Modern scholarship dates its composition to about the year 500. The exposition follows the text as the Church received it and gives the modern dating only where a historical claim depends on it; the authority of its teaching rests on that reception.

##### Rights.

Project prose, tables, and gradings are released under the licence stated in the colophon. Extended quotations are from public-domain editions and translations. Official documents of the Holy See and modern translations are quoted briefly, with attribution. Postconciliar English liturgical texts are cited rather than reproduced. Received prayers are given only from identified editions.

##### Limits.

The fallen angels are treated as the treatise treats them. The rites, discipline, and pastoral practice of exorcism belong to the study *Catholic Exorcism: History, Discipline, and Pastoral Practice* in this collection. Nothing here judges a particular case, gives a method of deliverance, or makes any claim about a named person’s spiritual state. The teaching of other religions about spirits enters only where a Father’s argument requires it. Where the Catholic schools divide, each position is given with the school that teaches it.

##### Review.

This reference was composed with artificial-intelligence assistance, as the generation metadata records. No independent theological, clerical, or ecclesiastical review has been performed, and none is claimed. It carries no *nihil obstat* or *imprimatur*.
